study.title: Jonah 3 - Repentance in Nineveh and the Mercy of God
study.overview: In this chapter, God sends Jonah again to Nineveh, and the prophet finally obeys. The message is of imminent judgment, but the reaction of the city surprises: the inhabitants believe in God, fast, dress in sackcloth and humble themselves. The king accompanies this movement with a public decree of repentance, calling even the animals to participate in the sign of mourning. The culmination is that God sees the change of attitude of the city and abrogates the evil announced, showing that his threat had corrective purpose and that mercy responds to conversion.

outline.title: Renewed Call and Judgment Announcement
outline.explanation: The word of the LORD comes a second time to Jonah, showing that God persists in his commission. Jonah obeys and goes to Nineveh, described as a very large city. His preaching is direct and unbeaten: in forty days the city would be destroyed. The notes highlight that the message did not bring an explicit clause of repentance, although God himself desired conversion rather than destruction.

outline.title: Nineveh's reaction: faith, humiliation and crying
outline.explanation: The Ninevites believe in God and begin a general fast, from the greatest to the smallest. The king abandons the throne, clothed in sackcloth and sits in ashes, then orders people and animals to fast and cover themselves with sack. The decree also demands a cry to God and abandonment of evil way and violence, recognizing that only divine mercy can prevent ruin.

outline.title: God sees conversion and revokes the evil advertised
outline.explanation: The outcome presents the divine look at the attitude of the city. God sees that they have stranded from the evil way, and then does not execute the evil that he had announced. The notes explain that this does not alter the character of God or deny his knowledge, but shows that his threat was conditional and that his disposition included the possibility of mercy before repentance.

study.context: The chapter resumes the initial structure of the book: God calls Jonah and sends him to Nineveh. The notes indicate that Nineveh was an extremely large city, and one of them suggests that the expression may include the urban area and surroundings, and reflect the time required for the message to go through the entire city. The king of Nineveh may have been a local ruler or the king of Assyria himself using Nineveh as an administrative center. Nothing in the text requires details beyond that.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes three central theological truths. First, God speaks with authority and gives the prophet a faithful message to announce. Second, divine judgment does not exclude mercy; on the contrary, the warning aims to lead to repentance. Third, true repentance involves faith, public humiliation and abandonment of evil, not just words. The language of God is repented must be understood as a change of procedure in relation to the repentant city, not as moral instability or ignorance of the future. Thus, the text shows God's holiness against violence and its readiness to spare those who turn to him.

scholarViews.insight: Nineveh's greatness underscores God's desire to save a vast city, and the observation that Jonah's message did not bring an explicit clause of forgiveness shows that the prophet knew that God wanted mercy before repentance.
Jonah's preaching is understood as a faithful and solemn proclamation, without softening the message; the urgency of the proclamation suits a mission that deals with souls in danger.

questions: What does Jonah's late obedience teach about God's patience with his servants?
Why does the repentance of the Ninevites include such strong public signs, such as fasting and sackcloth?
How to distinguish between the threat of judgment and the real possibility of mercy in the way God treats sin?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to take the word of God seriously without trying to soften it, but also to believe that repentance is never useless before the Lord. A concrete application is to examine whether there are ways of violence, injustice or wickedness that need to be abandoned, and to respond with confession, fasting or other biblical form of proper humiliation, seeking God's mercy with sincerity. It also teaches not to despise people or cities that seem distant from God, for it can transform even the most unlikely.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not establish for sure whether Nineveh was only a city ruled by a local king or the capital used by the king of Assyria; therefore, this was presented as a possibility, not as a fact. There is also not enough basis in the notes to define exact geographic details of the expression "three days of path," so this point was treated cautiously. The way God repented must be read in the light of notes, as a change of action in response to human repentance, without concluding something about limitation in divine knowledge.
